faq.a: Yes, though less frequently; vigilance is needed after any dopamine blocker.
It improves outcomes but may be unavailable; aggressive cooling and fluids are essential regardless.
Only after full clinical resolution (usually ≥2 weeks) and with a different, low‑potency agent at a low dose.

exam: What immediate steps do you take when a patient on haloperidol develops high fever and rigidity? — Stop the drug, start cooling, give IV fluids, consider dantrolene.
How would you differentiate NMS from serotonin syndrome at the bedside? — Look for lead‑pipe rigidity and absent clonus (NMS) versus hyperreflexia and clonus (serotonin).
Why is bromocriptine preferred over dopamine agonists like levodopa in NMS? — Bromocriptine directly stimulates dopamine receptors without causing peripheral catecholamine surge.

A patient on chlorpromazine has a temperature of 39 °C, CK 800 U/L, and tachycardia. What severity stage is this and what level of care is indicated? — Moderate NMS; high‑dependency monitoring with fluids and cooling.
What infection common in East Africa must be ruled out before confirming NMS? — Malaria, because it can cause fever and altered mental status.
Explain why anticholinergic drugs worsen NMS. — They further block central cholinergic pathways, increasing hyperthermia and rigidity.
If CK testing is unavailable, what clinical sign suggests severe muscle breakdown? — Dark, tea‑coloured urine indicating myoglobinuria.

What long‑term strategy prevents recurrence of NMS in a patient needing antipsychotic therapy? — Use the lowest effective dose of a low‑potency agent, titrate slowly, and educate staff on early signs.
ai.title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A life‑threatening reaction to dopamine‑blocking drugs characterised by hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental status. Prompt recognition and supportive care are essential, especially where intensive resources are limited.

b: Fever ≥38 °C (often >40 °C)
Lead‑pipe muscle rigidity
Fluctuating blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis
Elevated CK (often >1000 U/L) but may be unavailable
sections.p: NMS is an acute, idiosyncratic syndrome caused by dopamine antagonism. Diagnosis is clinical, using the Levenson or DSM‑5 criteria: fever, severe rigidity, autonomic dysfunction, and altered consciousness after exposure to a neuroleptic.

b: Mild – treat on general ward with close vitals
Moderate – consider high‑dependency unit, aggressive fluid resuscitation
Severe – ICU, possible mechanical ventilation, renal replacement
sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement: mild (fever, rigidity), moderate (CK rise, renal impairment), severe (hyperthermia >40 °C, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure). Staging guides intensity of monitoring.

b: High‑potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine)
Low‑potency typical antipsychotics (chlorpromazine)
Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine) – less frequent
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine (anti‑emetics)
Rapid dose escalation or parenteral route
sections.p: Any dopamine‑blocking agent can trigger NMS; typical agents are most common in low‑resource settings.

b: Sudden onset (hours‑days) after drug change
“Lead‑pipe” rigidity, especially neck and trunk
Autonomic storm: tachycardia, labile BP, tachypnea
Confusion, agitation or coma
sections.p: The patient often appears suddenly ill, lying in bed, with a rigid, board‑like posture, sweating, and a rapidly rising temperature.
Investigations confirm organ dysfunction and rule out mimics; when a test is unavailable, rely on bedside clues.

t.b: Is there muscle breakdown? – CK >1000 U/L supports NMS; if unavailable, look for dark urine and muscle pain.
Detect leukocytosis, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis.
Assess acute kidney injury from myoglobin; if labs missing, monitor urine colour and output.
Identify hepatic stress; elevations are common but non‑specific.
Exclude sepsis, malaria or TB as alternative causes of fever.

b: Temperature >40 °C – risk of rhabdomyolysis, DIC
CK >5000 U/L – severe muscle breakdown, renal failure
Acute respiratory distress – need for ventilation
Cardiac arrhythmias from electrolyte shifts
sections.p: Complications arise from hyperthermia, rigidity and organ failure; early detection saves lives.

b: Immediate discontinuation of neuroleptic and any dopamine‑blocking anti‑emetic
Aggressive IV fluids (30 ml/kg bolus then maintenance) to protect kidneys
Cooling measures: tepid sponging, antipyretics, ice packs; avoid NSAIDs if renal risk
Avoid anticholinergics (e.g., benztropine) – they worsen hyperthermia
sections.p: Stop the offending drug, provide intensive supportive care, and use specific pharmacologic antagonists when available.

b: Gradual re‑introduction of antipsychotic only after 2 weeks, using low‑potency agents
Document NMS episode in patient record; alert future prescribers
Educate nurses to monitor temperature and rigidity after any neuroleptic dose change
sections.p: After recovery, reassess psychiatric medication and educate staff on early signs.

b: Serotonin syndrome – hyperreflexia, clonus, diarrhoea; usually from serotonergic drugs
Malignant hyperthermia – triggered by anaesthetic agents, occurs intra‑operatively
Septic shock – source of infection, often with hypotension rather than hypertension
sections.p: Several acute syndromes mimic NMS; distinguishing features guide correct treatment.

b: CK may be normal in the first 12 h; rely on clinical rigidity
Leukocytosis can be absent in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV)
Fever may be blunted in patients on antipyretics or with adrenal insufficiency
sections.p: Certain labs may be normal early, leading to false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling urine output or dark urine
